chapters.headline: The Trampled Land
chapters.text:
The Trampled Land. I saw a nation sunk in grief
I heard a nation's wail;
And their deep toned misery was caught
By every passing gale.
Want guarded every peasant's door,
Swept each mechanic's board
I saw the nobles of that land
In pride and pomp roll by;
And I read Contempt for the poor man's lot
In every laughing eye.
I heard the infant's cry for bread
The mother's piercing shriek,
And I marked the trace of famine in
The father's sunken cheek.
I saw him cast his eye to heaven,
With a stern and sad appeal,
And I knew he felt that anguish deep
Which the hopeless only feel;
Yet still the nobles of that land
In pride and pomp rolled by,
Nor less contempt for the poor man's lot
Marked every haughty eye!
The people humbly sued for bread,
But their rulers gave a stone;
And they steel'd their sordid hearts and mocked
The peasant's dying groan!
Low rents cheap bread, the people cried
Untrammel labor's hands!
Tax'd corn, high rents, low wages, sneered
The callous ruling hands!
And the landlords of that land rolled by
To church in pomp and pride;
And the people's dying wail despised;
And the people's power defied!
Then madness came upon the land,
Twas the madness of despair;
Unarmed crowds went forth to beg
With shouts that rent the air!
And the rulers grinned a ghastly smile
Of triumph and delight,
As forth their minions came to crush
The weak with armed might;
And the landlords of that land surveyed,
With bland approving eye,
The savage and the ruthless war
Of stern monopoly
Now the council of that nation sits
Again in grave divan,
But care they aught for liberty?
Or for the rights of man!
A coxcomb's proclamations claim
Discussion fierce and strong.
But a starving nation's loud appeals
unclear pass along!
And still the cumberers of the earth
Contrive to hold in chains,
The nerve and sinew of the land
Throughout their wide domains.

chapters.headline: "If my Husband were to do so,"
chapters.text:
"If my Husband were to do so,". Poor woman! What a thousand pities it is for her! said Mrs. Grimes with feeling. I wonder now she stands it. If my husband were to do so it would kill me.
I could never stand it in the world, added Mrs. Pitts. It is a dreadful situation for a woman to be placed in. Mr. Larkin used to be one of the best of men. For years there was not a happier woman in town than his wife; but now it makes one's heart ache to look at her.
All I've got to say, spoke up Mrs. Peters, with a warmth, is, that I don't pity her much. Any woman who will live with a drunken husband, don't deserve pity. Why don't she leave him?
That is easier said than done, Mrs. Peters.
If my husband were to do so, I reckon him and me would part before twenty-four hours.
Mrs. Peters's husband was a most excellent man and a sober man. The sketch continues after a political / hard-cider meeting: he comes home late, pretends to be drunk, is put to bed, then whispers the title line. She boxes his ears. Later discussions end when he repeats the line.

chapters.headline: EDUCATION
chapters.text:
Next up — Page 1, Column 3. EDUCATION. Every boy should have his head, his heart and his hand educated. Let this truth never be forgotten.
By the proper education of his head, he will be taught what is good and what is evil, what is wise and what is foolish, what is right and what is wrong. By the proper education of the heart, he will be taught to love what is good, wise, and right, and to hate what is evil, foolish and wrong; and by the proper education of the hand, to add to his comforts, and to assist those that are around him.
The highest objects of a good education are to reverence and obey God, and to love and serve mankind.

chapters.headline: THE SEA
chapters.text: THE SEA. The natives of Central India have the most terrible ideas of the sea and the countries beyond it. Sir John Malcolm relates that when Cheeto, the Pindarrie chief, was flying from the English, he would not surrender for fear of transportation. A mangled body was later found in a tiger's lair, identified by sword, ornamented saddle, letter-case, and a general's commission from the ex-Rajah of Nagpoor.

chapters.headline: A HUMOROUS STORY
chapters.text:
A HUMOROUS STORY. From Brantz Mayer's Mexico.
A learned Judge in Mexico missed his repeater, thought he had left it under his pillow, and later found his wife had already sent it -- first with a man who brought a turkey (a thief), then with a supposed clerk who said the thief had been arrested. Watch and turkey both gone.

chapters.headline: TRADING WIVES
chapters.text: TRADING WIVES. A transaction a few miles of this place: Henry Adams and Jacob Eusperger, both mutually dissatisfied with their wives, made an exchange. Adams received about four hundred and twenty dollars in the bargain. Eusperger took Adams's children, four in number, and received his title to a small farm. Adams has taken Eusperger's wife and two of his children. Destination said to be the north of Indiana. Eusperger lived a few days with Adams's wife; a proceeding was lodged before I. J. Kelley, Esq.. Eusperger eluded officers; Mrs. Adams was taken and discharged for informality. Eusperger still in the neighborhood; measures being taken to secure him.

chapters.headline: LETTER OF T. W. BARTLEY
chapters.text:
LETTER OF T. W. BARTLEY. [K. Mabary?, Esq.]: Will you please insert, in the columns of the Ohio Statesman, the following letter.
Yours, very respectfully,
T. W. BARTLEY.
February 28th, 1844.
Senate Chamber,
February 20, 1844.
His Excellency, Wilson Shannon:
Dear Sir: It is with feelings of astonishment and regret, that I have read your letter of the 15th instant, addressed to Dr. John Dunham, editor of the St. Clairsville Gazette on the vexed question of the banks and the currency.

chapters.headline: Page 2, Columns 1-4
chapters.text:
Next up — Page 2, Columns 1-4. Page 2, Columns 1-4. Continuation and close of T. W. Bartley's letter to Gov. Wilson Shannon.
Points actually present in the OCR:
- Why not give objections to the law careful consideration and remove them? Bartley says that has been done; the House is Whig and could not amend this session.
- Banks of issue convert promissory notes into the money of the country. Adam Smith quoted: the most effectual means of fertilizing the rich man's field with the sweat of the poor man's brow.
- Banking as a political engine; subsidizing the press.
- Thirteen banks expired after the original act, two more after the amendatory act; they refused Democratic safeguards.
- Ohio stocks in New York risen from between 73 and 80 percent to 105 percent.
- Foreign / wild cat / rattlesnake / red dog paper and Pennsylvania relief notes.
- Shannon's argument that banks paid $183,117.00 tax from 1831 (thirteen years). Bartley answers that bank capital is taxed on dividends, other property on capital.
- U.S. Treasury report (1841) on national bank losses. Exchange and Trade Register figures for 1837-1842: bank circulation and deposits $34,000,000; bank capital failed and depreciated $248,000,000; state stock $100,000,000; company stock $60,000,000; real estate $300,000,000; total $782,000,000.
- The Wooster Bank bill: Bartley says it does not fully impose individual liability (exception for depositors); no mode of enforcement; stock transfer ends liability; specie clause allows Atlantic-city deposits / sight drafts; penitentiary clause is only ordinary embezzlement.
- Closing: he differs on points of vital interest but respects Shannon's motives.
Yours, with great respect,

chapters.headline: MR. STONE, OF THE COMMERCIAL ADVERTISER
chapters.text:
Next up — Page 2, Column 5. MR. STONE, OF THE COMMERCIAL ADVERTISER. Attack on William L. Stone's British partiality. Then a long extract on Martin Van Buren's conduct in the War of 1812 / De Witt Clinton nomination.
Letter of inquiry:
Avon, Livingston county, N. Y.
February 24, 1844.
Wm. L. Stone, esq.
Sir: what were the opinions and conduct of Martin Van Buren in the early stages of the war of 1812; on what grounds did he support De Witt Clinton for the presidency in opposition to Mr. Madison?
[ISAAC WELLS.]
Stone's published answer: Clinton nominated 26 May, nearly a month before the declaration of war; Van Buren not then a sitting member; after war was declared no public man in the State supported it more thoroughly; charge of opposition to the war itself is not true.
Hammond's Political History of New York quoted in support.

chapters.headline: Correspondence
chapters.text:
Next up — Page 2, Column 6. Correspondence. (via Cleveland Plaindealer / Statesman)
Cleveland, February 22, 1844.
To Col. David Tod:
Do you believe the interests of the people of the State of Ohio require the establishment of any kind of Banks by Legislative enactments; and, if so, what would you propose?
C. WINSLOW,
J. W. GRAY,
GEO. T. BARNUM,
E. HOSMER,
S. CURRIER,
Democratic Central Committee.
Warren, Trumbull co. Ohio,
February 27, 1844.
Gentlemen: First, then, I do believe that the interests of the people of Ohio require the establishment of banks by Legislative enactments. The old system of banking, with the following inserted, I have supposed, and still do think, would be the best for the people of Ohio:
1st The payment of the stock of the Bank in Gold and Silver.
2nd Individual liability on the part of the stock-holders for all the debts of the Bank.
3rd Limit the issues of the bank to three times the amount of specie.
4th Limit the loans, to the officers and stock holders, to at least one half of their stock.
5th Provide severe penalties, for all frauds on the part of the officers of the banks.
Respectfully yours,

chapters.headline: VALEDICTORY
chapters.text:
VALEDICTORY. With the present No. our connection with the KAY-diz Sentinel ceases. We have disposed of the establishment to L. HARPER, Esq., who will conduct it in future. Mr. Harper has been a citizen of KAY-diz since last summer; a practicing attorney and a practical printer. In 1838 he conducted the Democratic paper of Jefferson county in this State, and in 1840 he had sole control, as editor, of the Crawford Democrat (Crawford county, Pa.). Subscription: a dollar and a half. The outgoing editor has held the relation more than seven years.
Gov. Shannon's nomination as Minister to Mexico has not yet been confirmed. If he accepts, the vacancy in the Gubernatorial chair will be filled by Thomas W. Bartley, speaker of the Senate, whose ability may be judged of by his letter in to-day's paper.

chapters.headline: PENNSYLVANIA
chapters.text:
PENNSYLVANIA. Senate Chamber, Harrisburg, Pa., March 6, 1844.
Democratic State Convention: Hon. H. A. Muhlenburg for Governor (third ballot). Van Buren for President on first ballot, ninety-one votes; Col. Johnson thirty-five; Lewis Cass one. Johnson nominated by acclamation for Vice President.
JOHN S. McCAHEN.
Messrs. Blair and Rives.

chapters.headline: THE LAST WHIG NOMINATION
chapters.text:
THE LAST WHIG NOMINATION. Whig portion of the Legislature, assisted by a few lawyers from the country, on the 22d ult., nominated Mordecai Bartley, of Richland county, for Governor. [Bartley/Hartley], Speaker of the Senate. Thomas W. Bartley is the speaker named on page 3.
Ex-Gov. Corwin first choice (State Convention, 10 January) and refused. David Spangler second choice and declined. Nominee described as once a silent member of Congress, dropped by his constituents, not mentioned in public print for twelve or fourteen years. Plaindealer.
